lesson.title: How Much Should Results Bounce Around? Binomial Spread
lesson.summary: The standard deviation formula, the square root of np(1-p), measures how much a binomial count typically bounces around its mean, and unlike the mean it genuinely depends on the trials being independent.
lesson.body:
The mean of a binomial distribution, np, told you where the distribution is centered. The standard deviation tells you how spread out it typically is around that center, and its formula is SD(X) = the square root of np(1 minus p).

Unlike the mean formula, which holds even if the trials were somehow dependent, this formula genuinely needs independence. Variance behaves differently from expected value: the variance of a sum of random variables equals the sum of their individual variances only when those variables are independent, because otherwise you would also need to account for how the trials move together. Each individual trial, thought of as a 1 or 0 indicator of success, has variance p(1 minus p). Summed across n independent trials, that gives Var(X) = np(1 minus p), and taking the square root gives the standard deviation.

Return to the 3 coin flip distribution one more time: P(X=0)=1/8, P(X=1)=3/8, P(X=2)=3/8, P(X=3)=1/8, with mean 1.5. Computing variance directly from its definition, the average squared distance from the mean: (0 minus 1.5)^2 x 1/8 = 2.25/8 = 0.28125, (1 minus 1.5)^2 x 3/8 = 0.25 x 3/8 = 0.09375, (2 minus 1.5)^2 x 3/8 = 0.25 x 3/8 = 0.09375, and (3 minus 1.5)^2 x 1/8 = 2.25/8 = 0.28125. Adding these four pieces: 0.28125 + 0.09375 + 0.09375 + 0.28125 = 0.75. The formula gives the identical result: np(1 minus p) = 3 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.75. Taking the square root, SD(X) = the square root of 0.75, which is about 0.866.

For the 20 question true or false quiz from the last chapter, p = 0.5 and n = 20, so Var(X) = 20 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 5, and SD(X) = the square root of 5, about 2.236. Combining this with the mean from before, a student guessing randomly on all 20 questions would typically score somewhere in the neighborhood of 10 correct, give or take about 2.24, not exactly 10 every time, but rarely wildly far from it either.
